capabilities.target: private repositories accessible via the user's GitHub personal access token

inputs.source: Issues opened by anyone on GitHub in the user's public repository

controls.name: Client tool call approval prompt
controls.decay_rationale: The client asks for approval per tool call, but arguments are collapsed by default and users approve many calls per session, so the reviewer effectively sees a model-framed summary rather than the raw action. A more capable model can produce more persuasive or selectively incomplete summaries, and approval quality also decays with volume.

controls.name: Pin or hash MCP tool definitions for the GitHub server
controls.decay_rationale: Missing recommended structural control against post-approval tool definition changes.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1): public issue content can drive private repo reads and exfiltration into a public pull request

attack_path.note: Untrusted issue text is reachable because the user's task is to inspect open issues in a public repository.
The MCP server can read private repositories using a PAT with repo scope across all user-owned repositories.
A public pull request can disclose retrieved private content to an attacker-readable destination.

threat_refs.name: Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation

forecast.watch_signal: Model id/version change, approval UX changes, rising approvals per reviewer per day, or removal/narrowing of the per-call tool approval prompt.

evidence.observation: Anyone on GitHub can open issues in the public repository, so issue content is an untrusted source.
The design uses the github MCP server via a local docker command, exposing GitHub tool capabilities to the desktop agent.
The personal access token has repo scope across every repository the user owns, public and private, so private repository reads are in scope and credential scope is broad.
The client asks for approval per tool call, but arguments are collapsed by default and users approve many calls per session, so the approval gate is model_summary in practice rather than raw_action.
The initial trusted prompt is "Have a look at the open issues in my public repo.", which creates a plausible workflow in which untrusted issue text is brought into context before tool use.

recommendations.action: Replace broad repo-scope PAT access with credentials scoped only to the intended public repository and remove private-repository read access from this agent session.
Bind approval to raw tool arguments and destination details from the system of record; do not collapse arguments by default for read_private_repo or create_pr_public.
Treat public issue content as untrusted data only and prohibit any issue-authored instructions from influencing repository selection or outbound PR content unless the human explicitly confirms both.

findings.title: Confused deputy (TC4): broad personal access token lets public-repo content induce actions with authority broader than the requester's intent

attack_path.note: Attacker-controlled issue text enters the agent context.
The read capability operates with a PAT that spans all repositories the user owns.

forecast.watch_signal: PAT scope widens, new repository grants are added, the per-call approval prompt is weakened or removed, or the model version changes while approval remains summary-based.

evidence.observation: The PAT has repo scope across every repository the user owns, public and private, which is broader than the specific task of reviewing public repository issues.
Anyone on GitHub can author public issues, so an untrusted party can influence the agent while it holds broad credentials.
Tool approval is per call, but the reviewer sees collapsed arguments by default and approves many calls per session.

recommendations.action: Use least-privilege GitHub credentials restricted to the single public repository under review, ideally separating read-public-issues from any private-repository access.
Add repository allowlisting at the client or tool wrapper so issue-review sessions cannot invoke get_file_contents outside the named public repository without an explicit separate workflow.

findings.title: Agentic supply chain vulnerability: unpinned GitHub MCP server definitions allow post-approval tool rug pull or poisoning

attack_path.note: Remote-sourced container image defines the MCP server tools available to the client.
A changed tool definition can alter how or when sensitive reads are proposed.
A changed tool definition can steer public PR creation or mask payload details.

threat_refs.name: Publish Poisoned AI Artifacts: AI Agent Tools

forecast.watch_signal: MCP client config diff, container image/tag change, or new server entries without pinned definitions and verified identity.

evidence.observation: The MCP server is launched from a container image reference without any pinned digest or definition hash.
The design evidence does not show server identity verification or tool definition pinning for the GitHub MCP server.

recommendations.action: Pin the GitHub MCP server image by digest and pin or hash approved tool definitions so later changes cannot alter the reviewed capability surface silently.
Verify MCP server identity for remote-sourced artifacts before use and review tool descriptions for hidden instructions or schema changes on every update.

rating.rationale: Manual validation applied against the checklist because scripts could not be run. Present design shows a critical inherent path from untrusted public GitHub issues to broad private-repository reads and irreversible public PR egress. The declared per-tool approval gate lowers those path findings to moderate under the rubric because it is wired as an approval gate, but the overall residual remains high due to the separate present supply-chain finding: the GitHub MCP server is unpinned and peer identity is not verified. Forecast is critical because the summary-style approval prompt is the single control whose decay or removal most increases risk; under model_upgrade, autonomy_increase, longer_task_horizon, or control_removal, the exfiltration and confused-deputy findings return to critical.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration artifacts provided here, not observed runtime behavior, live tool manifests, or empirical exploit testing.
No system prompt, full tool manifest, tool schemas, or runtime traffic were provided, so capability scope and approval UX details are assessed from the stated stable ids and runtime notes.
Auth method and server identity details for the GitHub MCP connection were not fully specified; protocol findings therefore assume only what is evidenced in the provided configuration.
